0: The most common mistake when choosing a model is treating public leaderboards as conclusions. A leaderboard measures "how a model performs on a standard set of questions," but what you need to answer is "whether the model is good enough for my business." The two are related, but not equivalent. This chapter presents an evaluation method that can be run in half a day and whose conclusions can be reviewed.
1: First, distinguish three types of evaluation
2: Different evaluation goals call for completely different approaches. Mixing them together leads to the gap of "ranked first on the leaderboard but unusable in production."
3: Capability evaluation: whether the model can solve a certain type of problem. Use public benchmarks or self-built question sets; what you look at is the upper bound.
4: Scenario evaluation: whether the model meets the bar on your business data. Use a test set with the real distribution; what you look at is the lower bound.
5: System evaluation: whether the entire pipeline is stable after retrieval, tools, and moderation are connected. What you look at is latency, failure rate, and cost.
6: In the model selection phase, first run capability evaluation to narrow the range, then use scenario evaluation to make the final decision, and leave system evaluation until before launch. Skipping the second step is the most common cause of project rework.
8: Public benchmarks are suitable for coarse screening, not for acceptance. The following are common choices; when using them, you need to know what each one actually measures.
11: What to watch out for when using it
14: The questions are exam-style and differ greatly from business phrasing
17: Limited explanatory power for Chinese scenarios
20: Check whether the reasoning chain is stable, not just the final answer
23: Pass rate is noticeably affected by prompt format
26: Closest to the format constraints in the product
27: There are three details worth tracking when looking at leaderboards: whether the version number corresponds to the weights you have, whether the evaluation uses zero-shot or few-shot, and whether the scores come with confidence intervals. For leaderboards that report only a point estimate, the sample size is often insufficient to distinguish adjacent ranks.
28: Run a local evaluation with EvalScope
29: EvalScope is an evaluation framework in the ModelScope ecosystem. Its advantages are configuration-driven setup, support for local models and API models, and results that can be saved as structured files. Below is a minimal working command.
30: Three parameters are worth explaining. --limit first runs the pipeline with a small sample to confirm everything works before scaling to the full set; --work-dir saves per-question results for reviewing incorrect answers; the model name should specify an exact version, not an alias like latest. After running, look at the distribution of incorrect answers first, then the total score—two models with the same total score but different types of errors may be completely different in your scenario.
32: The scenario test set does not need to be large, but it must come from the real distribution. A rule of thumb is 100 to 300 items per key task, covering three categories: high-frequency, long-tail, and adversarial samples. The construction order is as follows.
33: Sample from online logs or tickets, and keep the original expressions; do not rewrite them to be more "standard."
34: Write a reference answer for each sample, and annotate the tolerance range (which differences are acceptable).
35: At least two people annotate independently; arbitrate disputed samples separately, and record the reasons for arbitration.
36: Set aside 20% as a holdout set, which must not be used when tuning prompts.
37: If the data cannot leave the domain, run open-source models locally; if you need to compare with closed-source APIs, upload only desensitized samples and confirm that the terms of service permit it.
38: Scorer: don't use just one metric
39: Scoring for generative tasks is the most prone to distortion. It is recommended to keep both automatic metrics and manual spot checks; when the two disagree, manual judgment prevails.
40: For extraction tasks, use field-level precision and recall, and count null values separately.
41: For classification tasks, use a confusion matrix, focusing on the error direction that the business cares about most.
42: For generative tasks, use a three-item rubric of "key point coverage + factual errors + format compliance," with manual scoring from 1 to 5.
43: For agent tasks, use task completion rate, tool call accuracy, and privilege escalation rate; the privilege escalation rate must be listed separately.
44: Automatic metrics can use a model as a judge, but the judge model must be from a different family than the evaluated models, and it must be calibrated once on a manually annotated subset. When the judge and the evaluated model come from the same source, scores will be systematically inflated.
45: Write the results as a table that supports decisions
46: The value of an evaluation report lies in supporting decisions, not in listing scores. It is recommended to put one candidate model per row, list the following columns, and write a one-sentence conclusion at the end.
52: Mean and confidence interval of the primary metric
54: Incidence of the most unacceptable type of error
56: Tokens and cost per call, or local VRAM usage
58: P50 and P95, not the average
62: Data contamination: test set questions appear in the training corpus, inflating scores. Use recent samples and deduplicate.
63: Prompt inequivalence: carefully tuning prompts for model A while using the default template for model B makes the comparison meaningless.
64: Inconsistent sampling parameters: different temperature, top_p, and max length make results incomparable.
65: Sample size too small: differences among a few dozen samples may just be noise; at minimum, look at confidence intervals.
66: Looking only at average scores: averages mask long-tail failures, and the long tail is often the source of production incidents.
67: Ignoring version drift: API models are updated without notice, so evaluation conclusions should be dated and rerun periodically.
68: Evaluation is not a one-time action but a continuously running pipeline. Put the test set, scoring scripts, and result reports together in the repository; the next time you switch models, you only need to rerun it once.
